summary.title: Your URL Is Your State
summary.one_liner: URLs can hold app state (filters, views, selections) so pages are shareable, bookmarkable and restorable, and this article shows which state belongs there and how to manage it with plain JavaScript and React.
keywords: single page app state lost on refresh
takeaways: Use path segments for hierarchy, query parameters for filters and options, and fragments for in-page positions.
Put state in the URL when someone else opening the link should see the same view; keep sensitive data, transient UI and large nested state out.
Use pushState for undoable navigation (filters, pagination) and replaceState for refinements like search-as-you-type; debounce frequent updates.
Omit default values from URLs and handle defaults in code; choose clear, consistent parameter names.
Handle popstate (or your router) so the UI stays in sync with the Back and Forward buttons.
summary.summary: The article argues that URLs are a underused state container, using examples such as a PrismJS configuration link, GitHub line highlighting, Google Maps and e-commerce filters to show how a single URL can restore a full UI. It explains what each URL part (path, query, fragment) is suited for, and gives a heuristic for deciding which state belongs in the URL. Code samples show reading and updating parameters with URLSearchParams, handling popstate, and using useSearchParams in React Router and Next.js. It closes with best practices and anti-patterns such as storing passwords, base64-encoded config blobs and memory-only SPA state.
